newsitem.title: KENYA: Regional wars seen hurting Ugandan business.
newsitem.headline: Regional wars seen hurting Ugandan business.

text.p: Civil wars in eastern Zaire, southern Sudan and rebel activity in parts of Uganda have cut trade and undermined manufacturing but Uganda's finance minister says that the east African country is not on its death-bed.
"Uganda won't die -- but we shall definitely have to work harder next year," Finance Minister Jehoash Mayanja-Nkangi told reporters responding to concerns that the war had hit growth.

Ugandan manufacturers say their markets in eastern Zaire and southern Sudan have dried up because fighting has rendered the areas too dangerous. They said northern and southwestern Uganda were also not fully accessible and fighting increased poverty.
On Wednesday, the privately-owned The Monitor daily newspaper said manufacturers of soap, cooking oils, plastics, detergents, cigarettes, cement and steel were hardest hit.
It listed main business centres of Bunia, Butembo, Goma, Beni and Arua in Zaire or Sudan or along the borders as former major recipients of Ugandan goods now unable to consume any.
Uganda estimated its gross domestic product (GDP) growth at 7.8 percent in 1995/96. It has not given 1996/97 estimates.
Government financial experts said they expected a slump in business because of the regional wars and internal strife.
They added that a traders' strike last year against Value Added Tax (VAT) had exacerbated the situation.

Traders in southwestern Uganda said there were no Zaireans to purchase their food crops or manufacturered products and as a result they received little or no gold or other metals that normally trickled into Uganda throughout the year.
The Monitor quoted the executive director of leading manufacturer Mukwano Industries as saying that production of cooking oils, plastics and soap had been drastically reduced.
"There has been a complete slowdown for the past six months. We have reduced production by 30 percent," the director said.
Other manufacturers reported the same problems.
Most food and urgent relief requirements come in by way of international donor assistance from Southern Africa, the United States and Europe, according to charities working in Uganda.

On Tuesday, the Famine Early Warning System (FEWS) said that in northern Uganda, the effects of massacres and mass kidnappings by the rebel Lord's Resistance Army and the West Nile Bank Front had disrupted food production and trade.

"Many residents of Arua, Nebbi, Moyo, Gulu and Kitgum districts were unable to tend their fields during the second season or to complete harvesting of whatever crops they managed to cultivate," FEWS, a project of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), said in a report in Nairobi.

It said that following the most recent wave of violence in the hardest hit districts of Gulu and Kitgum, the U.N. food aid agency WFP estimated that 220,000 people out of an approximated population of 849,900 were affected by the conflict.
Tour operators said visits to the gorilla parks or other centres in the southwest were undermined by the war situation.
Last week, the IMF gave its stamp of approval for a debt relief plan for Uganda, making it the first candidate of a new international initiative to help the poorest countries.
That decision would lead to a reduction in Uganda's debt of about $385 million of a total $3.4 billion external debt.
